newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Scrappy Bhutto vows to retake power in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Scrappy Bhutto vows to retake power in Pakistan.

text.p: Pakistan's ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto, girding for a protracted political battle, has promised to fight her dismissal in court and recapture power.
"I'm an elected prime minister and I'll be prime minister again," she said in her first public remarks since President Farooq Leghari sacked her in a pre-dawn order on Tuesday.
A truculent Bhutto told reporters on Wednesday that she would mount a legal challenge against Leghari's order, which said corruption, nepotism and misrule had paralysed her government.

"We expect the court to restore the (National) Assembly within a month," she told a packed news conference in the prime minister's residence, where police had kept her in custody for 36 hours before lifting curbs on her movements.
Bhutto accused Leghari of ordering the kidnapping of her husband, a businessman and former investment minister, who was detained in the provincial capital Lahore on Tuesday.

"I believe that my husband Asif Ali Zardari...has been kidnapped on your orders since yesterday morning," she said in a hand-written letter to Leghari, copies of which were distributed at her news conference.
Pakistan's new caretaker government led by Meraj Khalid said it had lifted restrictions on Bhutto's movements but Zardari was still in custody for reasons it did not fully explain.
Zardari is the target of corruption allegations levelled against Bhutto's government. He has denied any wrongdoing.
"Asif Zardari is in protective custody. It means there is something against him, some inquiry may be on, or something else may be considered," Information Minister Irshad Haqqani said.
Bhutto's pledge to fight to the finish added fresh uncertainty to an already turbulent political scene.

Calling on voters to elect "honest, able and God-fearing people", Leghari on Tuesday set general elections for next February. But the timetable could be upset by Bhutto's legal challenge, which seemed sure to prolong the political crisis.
A confident Bhutto noted that the Supreme Court had reinstated the government of her main political opponent Nawaz Sharif after it had been dismissed by then president Ghulam Ishaq Khan in 1993.
"I will go to the court expecting justice," she said.
The United States said on Tuesday Bhutto's sacking appeared to be constitutional, and it joined most other countries in expressing hopes for continued good relations with Pakistan.

The whiff of fresh air generated by Bhutto's ouster gave a hefty boost to share prices on the Karachi stock exchange, where the benchmark index jumped 5.25 percent on hopes the new government would tackle corruption.
At its first meeting, Khalid's two-day-old caretaker government appealed to citizens to send evidence of corruption to the interior minister to aid in the fight against graft.
The cabinet also cut minister's salaries in half and barred them from travelling first class as part of an austerity package aimed at trimming spending and checking the "VIP culture".

On Wednesday afternoon, authorities lifted restrictions on Bhutto's movements which had kept her confined to the prime minister's official residence and prevented all but a trickle of visitors for 36 hours after she was sacked.
Bhutto said the whole of Pakistan was mourning her dismissal, but there were few signs of unrest, while supporters of opposition parties were jubilant and gearing up for elections.

In Islamabad, police detained about two dozen Bhutto followers who protested against her ouster. But they were many fewer than the thousands who turned out in the city's streets last week to protest against Bhutto's government.
